A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mixture-of-Recursions work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across appendix and table renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training and evaluation results, inference-throughput measurements, and extensive routing, parameter-sharing and KV-caching ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds higher-budget evaluation and parameter-controlled experiments in Tables 7, 8 and 11.

M1.justification: The parameter-sharing schemes, expert-choice and token-choice routing, hierarchical filtering, losses and two KV-caching strategies remain unchanged. The added experiments vary configurations of the existing method; proposed larger non-shared blocks and depth-specific experts remain future work.

E1.justification: Both versions use FineWeb-Edu and the same six benchmark groups: LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, ARC and MMLU. The added experiments change compute budgets and model configurations, without introducing new tasks, domains or input conditions. The 1.7B base scale was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Vanilla and Recursive Transformers remain the evaluated baselines, and existing comparisons retain their comparator membership. The new controls reuse existing architectures and Cycle/Middle-Cycle sharing strategies. Newly cited methods such as ABBIE are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Beyond the retained 2/5/16.5e18 FLOP experiments, v3 adds a 68.5e18 FLOP comparison at the existing 1.7B scale. It also introduces distinct capacity controls: varying recursion at fixed 118M parameters and 10B tokens, and comparing sharing strategies at fixed 252M parameters and 10B tokens. These substantially extend the evaluation design without revising the original protocols.

E4.justification: New Table 8 tests whether additional recursion improves performance while unique parameter count stays fixed. New Table 11 tests Middle-Cycle versus Cycle with matched parameter counts, addressing the unequal capacities in v1's sharing comparison. These add substantive controls for two central architectural questions; the original routing, caching and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The isoFLOP appendix retains the same single-training/checkpoint-reuse description. Neither version supplies repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests, and v3 introduces no new seed or replication reporting.

E6.justification: Retained result tables have unchanged values, but Tables 7, 8 and 11 add consequential findings. At the new 68.5e18 budget, vanilla averages 48.9% versus 48.4% for two-recursion expert-choice MoR. At fixed 118M parameters, validation NLL falls from 2.9678 with one recursion to 2.9111 with three. The matched sharing comparison reports 42.32% for Middle-Cycle versus 41.90% for Cycle. These are additional conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Table 2 newly restricts its analytical cost comparison to recursion blocks, excluding non-shared layers; v1 described model-wide memory and IO ratios without this qualification. This is a limited correction to the cost model's stated scope. The formulas, routing definitions and other mathematical content remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract removes the claim that the KV-sharing variant is designed to decrease prefill latency, retaining its memory-saving purpose. The central contributions concerning unified parameter sharing, adaptive recursion and efficient caching, along with the broad performance claims in the introduction and conclusion, remain.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 replaces the interpretation that depth reflects a token's semantic importance with contextual predictability of the subsequent token. Sections 2.2.2 and 6 restrict prefill-skipping benefits to Cycle sharing. New Appendix C.1 acknowledges that vanilla's advantage at the higher budget may indicate scaling limitations, and Section 7.1 revises proposed scaling remedies. These substantially qualify mechanism explanations and applicability.

D1.justification: The additional experiments document parameter counts, training-token budgets and concrete layer arrangements, including 1+8×3+1 versus 10×3 effective layers for the matched sharing comparison. Existing hardware disclosures, general training and evaluation instructions, throughput implementation details and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to ABBIE, Adaptive Computation Time, Sparse Universal Transformer, Loop Neural Networks and DeepSpeed-MoE. These modestly expand the recursive-model context and support proposed future scaling directions; the main research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: The main section structure is preserved. Changes include localized rewrites of routing interpretation and scaling limitations, expanded acknowledgements, a new Appendix C with two subsections, and corresponding appendix relabeling. Most existing prose is retained with small language and formatting edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds three result tables, updates captions explaining routing visualizations and cost accounting, and relocates existing appendix material to accommodate the additions. Existing figures and retained table structures remain substantially unchanged, including the qualitative examples relabeled from Table 14 to Table 17.

improvement.justification: The parameter-matched controls strengthen the architectural evidence, while the higher-budget experiment candidly exposes a scaling limitation. Clarifying next-token routing interpretation and restricting prefill claims also improves accuracy. The gains remain limited: the new controls cover narrow settings, small differences lack uncertainty estimates, and broad abstract and conclusion claims are not fully reconciled with the new 1.7B results.
